script.opening_words: How to build wealth if you're already behind? I hear some version of this constantly. Someone's 38, they just found out their 24-year-old co-worker has more saved than they do, and they spend the rest of the work day quietly spiraling in a bathroom stall pretending to be on a phone call. That's not one person's story. That's basically a universal experience with a different age attached every time. Maybe you're 35 with a savings account that has less in
script.ending_words: reframe things for you, hit subscribe. I put out videos like this every week breaking down the stuff that actually moves the needle instead of just sounding good in a thumbnail. And if you want to go deeper with people who are doing exactly this, catching up, staying consistent, actually building something, the link to the community is right down in the description. I'll see you in the next one.
script.analysis: Full 20215 canonical characters read. A catch-up plan: hook (38-year-old vs 24-year-old co-worker); highlight-reel comparison; not starting is the costliest mistake; step one net worth; contribution rate and consistency over start date ($3,500/yr eating-out redirect at 10% for 30 years); income lever over cutting; debt sequencing (22% card, avalanche vs snowball); employer match; priority order; risk-chasing mistake (caller anecdote, 10% single-stock cap); late-starter at 45 using index funds; automation and raising contributions; tree-planting proverb; recap and community link. Verified: eating-out ~$4,000 (BLS $3,945 per household). The $600,000 figure holds only with monthly or start-of-year contributions ($575,729 year-end). Mostly advice; few checkable claims. The stored ending is complete.

claim_audit.assessment: [PRIMARY_SOURCE_DIRECTLY_INSPECTED] BLS Consumer Expenditures 2024 (USDL-25-1586, released 2025-12-19, before the 2026-08-29 upload): food away from home $3,945 per consumer unit. The figure matches, but it is per household (consumer unit), not per person.

claim_audit.assessment: [INDEPENDENT_CALCULATION_VERIFIED] Year-end annual contributions give $575,729 (below $600,000); start-of-year contributions give $633,302 and monthly contributions ($291.67 at 10%/12) give $659,309. "North of $600,000" holds only under the latter conventions; 10% is a nominal return, so the real value is far lower.
